And they cried out for fear] For fear of him, in whom was laid up all their comfort. But [ilegible] in dubijs Augur, Timor.-How oft are we mistaken, and befooled by our fears?

entries.title: Matthew 14:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He waits to be (Isa. 30. 18.) gracious: Our extremity is his opportunity. Cum duplicantur lateres venit Moses. God brings his people to the mount with Abraham, yea to the very brow of the hill, till their feet slip, and then delivers them: when all is given up for lost, then comes he in, ([ilegible].) as out of an engine.

It is I, fear not.] Quid timet homo in sinu Dei positus? A childe that is in his fathers bosome, fears no bugbears.

entries.title: Matthew 14:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This fact of Peter some extoll, as an argument of his strong faith and love to Christ. But others of better judgement, censure it as an effect of unbelief, and rashnesse in him, requiring to be confirmed by a miracle: to the which though our Saviour assented, yet we cannot say that he approved it. The other Disciples beleeved Christ upon his bare word, but Peter must have a signe. He had it, but with a check, ver. 31.

entries.title: Matthew 14:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Had the [ilegible] asked a signe, they should have gone without, and have heard, wicked and bastardly brood. as Matth. 12. 39. But a [ilegible] shall have it, rather then he shall [ilegible] betwixt two, as the word is, ver. 31. Christ condescends ([ilegible], [ilegible]) to his infirmity, and bids him, come. And the like was his dealing with that vertuous Gentle woman Mrs Honiwood: who [ilegible] much of her salvation, was often counselled by a worthy Minister, to take heed of enquiries further then Gods word, &c. Yet still did the temptation grow upon her, insomuch that having a Venice-[ilegible] in her hand, and the same Minister sitting by her, You have often told me, said she to him, that I must seek no further then Gods word. But I have been long without comfort, and (M. Boltons [ilegible] a right [ilegible]. [ilegible]. p. 5. out of [ilegible] his [ilegible]. of Hypoc pag 357.) can endure no longer. Therefore if I must be saved, let this glasse be kept from breaking; and so she threw it against the walls. The glasse rebounds again, and comes safe to the ground: which the Minister having gotten into his hands, saith, Oh repent of this sin, [ilegible] God for his mercy, and never distrust him more of his promise: for now have you his voice from heaven in a miracle, telling you plainly of your estate. This was curiosity, saith mine Authour, and might have brought dispair: Yet it was the Lords mercy to remit the fault, and grant an extraordinary confirmation [ilegible] her faith.

entries.title: Matthew 14:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Every bird can [ilegible] in a sun shine-day: and it is easie to swim in a warm bath: but to beleeve in an angry God, as David, in a killing God, as Iob, to stick to him in deepest desertion, as the Church, Psal. 44. 17, 18. to trust in his Name, and stay upon his word, where there is darknesse and no light, as Isa. 50. 10. to cast anchor even in the darkest night of temptation, when neither Sun nor stars appear, as Paul and his company, Acts 27. [ilegible]. praying still for day, and waiting till it dawne, O quam hoc non est omnium! this is not in the power of every Peter, who yet shall be graciously supported that they faint not, neither sink under the heaviest burden of their light afflictions. It was not so much the strength of the winde, as the weaknesse of his faith, that put Peter into this fit of fear. Be we faithfull in weaknesse, though weak in faith, and it shall go well with [ilegible]. Be as a ship at anchor, which though it move much, yet removes not at all.

entries.title: Matthew 14:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou petty-fidian, [ilegible]; Christ chides Peter, and yet helps him. Involuntary failings, unavoidable infirmities discard us not: as robberies done by Pirats of either Nation, break not the league between Princes: as [ilegible] not the marriage-[ilegible]. Christ knew us well before he took us, yet took us for better, for worse. 2. He hates putting away, Mal. 2. 16. and herein, as he is above law, so his mercy is matchlesse. Jer. 3. 1. Jehoshuah the High-Priest, though he was so ill-clothed, yet he stood before the Angel, Zech. 3. 3. Much will be born with where the fault is of passion meerly, or of [ilegible] and inadvertency, as here.

entries.title: Matthew 14:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As if it had been weary of [ilegible] so big, and now desired rest after hard labour; as the word here ([ilegible], [ilegible].) used importeth. Herodotus useth the same word in the same sense, where he speaks of a tempest layed by the Magicians. Rupertus calleth the windes the worlds beesoms, which are used by God to sweep his great house, and purge the ayr. If the Prince of ([ilegible]. in [ilegible], [ilegible].) the ayr make use of them to sweep Gods children, as he did Jobs children, out of the world, it cannot be said as 1 King. 19. 11. that God is not in that winde: sor he numbreth their hairs, and counts their flittings, and, being the great AEolus, layes laws upon (Virg [ilegible] [ilegible]. [ilegible] 1.) the windes and waves, which instantly obey him. No sooner was Christ in the ship, but they were all at land.

entries.title: Matthew 14:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not by Creation as Adam, and the Angels, Luk. 3. 38. Job 1. 6. Nor by Adoption as all beleevers, Joh. 1. 12. but 1 By eternall generation, Prov. 8 22. 2. By personall union, Psal. 2. 7.

entries.title: Matthew 14:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Where he presently found some that observed him. When God sets up a light in any place, a burning and a shining light, there is some work to be done. A husbandman would not send his servant with his sickle to reap thistles and nettles only. The ministery sent to a place, is an [ilegible] of some elect there, 2 Thes. 1. 5.

entries.title: Matthew 14:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See their charity. The Philistims were not so ambitious of sending the plague, together with the [ilegible], one to another, as these were of helping their neighbours to health, to heaven. We are born for the benefit of many, as [ilegible] Physitians told him, Non sibise, sed multorum ([ilegible]. Adam. [ilegible].) [ilegible] esse natum. Publike persons especially must have publike spirits. Kings have in Greek their names from healing: And [ilegible] ([ilegible] [ilegible].) are called Healirs, or binders up of wounds, Isa 3. 7.

entries.title: Matthew 14:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Oh the matchlesse might and [ilegible] of Christ our Saviour! He [ilegible] to [ilegible] infirmity, and heals them promiscuously, not once questioning their [ilegible]. He giveth to all men liberally, and hitteth no man in the ([ilegible]. 1 5.) teeth with his former failings, or present [ilegible]. Be we also, ([ilegible] [ilegible] [ilegible] to heal [ilegible], [ilegible].) by his example, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. This was the Philosophicall friendship of the Pythagoreans, the legall of the [ilegible] (a sect among the Jews, that had their names of healing) and should be most of all the Evangelicall friendship of us [ilegible]. Thou shalt be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer &c. Isa. 58. 12. A gallant tittle, better then a thousand [ilegible].

entries.title: Matthew 15:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
THen, when the men of Genne sareth favoured and observed him. Satan stomacketh the prosperity of Gods Kingdom in any place, and stirreth up his to oppose it. Esau began with Iacob in the womb, that no time might be lost. As soon as ever the Churches childe was borne, the devil sought to drown him, Rev. 12.

Scribes and Pharisees] Learned and lewd; these are Christs greatest enemies, hypocrites especially, those night-birds, that cannot bear the light of true religion, but, as bats, beat against it.

Which were of Ierusalem] That faithfull City was now become (Isa. 1. 22, [ilegible].) an harlot, her silver was degenerate into drosse, her wine mixt with water. The sweetest wine turns into the sowrest vineger, the whitest ivory burnt, into the [ilegible] coal. So about the year 1414 Theodoricus [ilegible] in Germany, an Augustine Frier complained, not without cause, Ecclesiam Romanam ex aureâ factam (Joh. [ilegible] [ilegible]. [ilegible]: 6) argenteam, ex argenteâ [ilegible], ex ferreâ terream, superesse [ilegible] in stercus [ilegible]. Machiavil observed, that there was no where ([ilegible]. [ilegible] de rep. lib. 1. cap [ilegible].) [ilegible] piety, then in those that dwelt nearest to Rome.

entries.title: Matthew 15:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They cryed up aloud Traditions, and the authority of Antiquity. Similem hodie dicam Papistae nobis scribunt. For as the Philosophers fled and hid themselves in the haereticks, as one saith, so did the Scribes and Pharisees in the Popish Doctours. Non tam ovum ovo simile: One egge or apple is not so like another, as Pharisees and Papists. The Pharisees deemed it as great a sin to eat with unwashen hands, ([ilegible]. Antiquit. Heb. [ilegible]. 49.) as to commit fornication. Semblably, the Papists count it worse to deface an Idol, then to kill a man, to eat flesh or eggs on a fasting day, then to commit incest, and for a Priest to have one wife then ten harlots. [ilegible], say some, is the number of the beast, 666. (Parcus in [ilegible].)

entries.title: Matthew 15:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He shapes them an answer by way of Recrimination: which is a singular means of conviction to the adversary, but hard to be done by us without some ([ilegible].) mixture of [ilegible], such as was that in David to Michal, 2 Sam. 6. 21.

Transgresse the Commandment of God by your tradition?] Gods commands should be kept as the apple of the eye, Prov. 7. 2. They are broken by omissions, commissions and failings in the manner: like as a man may miss: the mark by shooting short, or beyond, or wide. These Pharisees, as those Athenians of old ([ilegible]) (whereas they had most excellent Laws, but most [ilegible] natures) chose rather to live by their lusts, then by their laws. They had many traditions, and unwritten verities, pretended to be invented and prescribed them by their [ilegible], that by the [ilegible] thereof they might be the better [ilegible] to keep Gods Commandments. These traditions they stiled, Mashlamnathoth, Completions or Perfections: because ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible] [ilegible]) thereby they conceited, that the written law was made more complete and perfect. And say not the Papists as much of their traditions?

entries.title: Matthew 15:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This is called the first ([ilegible] 6. 2. [ilegible], [ilegible] an [ilegible].) Commandment with promise, viz. the first affirmative Commandment, or the first, in the second Table: or the first of all the tea with promise. For that in the second Commandment is rather a [ilegible] of Gods justice and mercy, and that to the observers of ([ilegible] D Gouge of [ilegible]. [ilegible].) the whole Law: but here is a particular promife made to them, that keep this particular commandment.

Honour thy father and mother] Among other good offices, nourish (Gen. 47. 12.) and cherish them as Joseph did Jacob and his family, [ilegible] (Ruth 4. 15.) ([ilegible] 5. 4.) [ilegible], as a man nourisheth his little-ones, lovingly and tenderly: ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. c. 23.) Be unto them as Obed was to Naomi, A restorer of her [ilegible], ([ilegible] b. [ilegible].) and a nourisher of her old age. This the Apostle commends to us, as ([ilegible] c. 6.) a [ilegible] not only good before men, [ilegible] acceptable before God. This the Stork and the Mouse teach us, by their singular love to their aged [ilegible]. [ilegible] was the staff of his fathers age, and thereby merited the honourable name of Scipio among the Romans. Epaminondas rejoyced in nothing more, then that he had lived to chear up the hearts of his aged parents, by the reports of his [ilegible]. ([ilegible].) Our parents are our houshold gods, said Hierocles. AEneas is sirnamed Pius, for his love to his father, whom he bore upon his [ilegible] out of the fire of Troy. And Aristotle tels how that when from the hill AEtna, there ran down a [ilegible] of fire that consumed ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) all the houses thereabouts, in the midst of those fearfull flames Gods speciall care of the godly shined most brightly. For the river of fire parted it self, and made a kinde of lane for those who ventured to rescue their aged parents, and pluck them out of the [ilegible] of death.

He that curseth father or mother] That giveth them an ill ([ilegible].) word, or but an ill look; for, Vultu saepe laeditur pietas. The (Prov 30. 17. [ilegible] veret [ilegible] gutture corvus. Catul.) eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young Eagles shall eat it. Now they are cursed with a witnesse, whom the holy Ghost thus curseth in such emphaticall manner, in such exquisite terms.

entries.title: Matthew 15:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The intollerable covetousnesse ([ilegible]. Sands his [ilegible]. [ilegible]. 4.) of the [ilegible] bred this abominable corruption of this Commandment, as it did many other like. See my Notes on John 2. 14, 15. By the same arts at this day the Lady of Loretto, as they call her, hath her Churches so stuffed with vowed presents and memories, as they are fain to hang their cloisters and Churchyards with them. The [ilegible] of grace in this Kingdom, had a man within it [ilegible] with an hundred wiers to make the image goggle with the eyes, nod with the head, hang the lip, move and shake his jaws according as the value was of the gift that was offered. If it were a small [ilegible] of silver, he would hang a frowning lip: if a piece of gold, then should his jaws go merrily. The (Act. and Mon. fol., 084.) like was done by the bloud of Hales, brought afterwards by the Lord Cromwell to Pauls crosse, and there proved to be the bloud of a duck.

It is a gift by whatsoever, &c.] Some read it thus, by Chorban, [ilegible] by this gift, if thou receive any profit by me: understand, then let (Godw. Antiq. [ilegible].) God do thus, and much more to me, q. d. by Chorban thou shalt receive no profit by me. Others thus, Chorban, Anathema ([ilegible], si [ilegible], ut Mat. 10. 14. & 23. 18. [ilegible].) sit, Be it a devoted thing whatsoever I may profit thee by, q. d. Being consccrated to God, it shall be beneficiall to us both, and not here only in this life, but hereafter in that to come: wheras cost bestowed upon parents soon vanisheth, and reacheth no further then the life presents.

entries.title: Matthew 15:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Supple, insons erit. Our Saviour contents himself to relate [ilegible] words only of the tradition, as Lawyers use to do the first words of the Statute or Canon, they [ilegible] te or argue upon.

Thus have you made the Commandment of none effect] Ye have ([ilegible] of [ilegible] & [ilegible] rule, authority.) sought to shoulder God out of his throne, to devest and spoil him of his rule and authority, to ungod him as it were, by making his Commandment void and invalid. And do not Papists as much as all this, whiles they teach that a Monk [ilegible] not leave his cloister, to relieve his father, but must rather see and suffer him to die for hunger in the streets? Lyra hath these very words, Filius [ilegible] professionem factam in religione, excusatur à subveniendo parenlibus. This Lyra was a famous English Jew, but an arrant Papist, as, for most part, all were then: for he flourished, Anno 1320.

entries.title: Matthew 15:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of such as you, and so of you too. The Prophets and Apostles then spake not of them only with whom they lived, and to whom they wrote (as the Jesuites blaspheme) but their oracles and doctrines do extend still to men of the same stamp and making. In the volume of thy book (Psal. 40. 7.) it is written of me, saith David: he found his own name in Gods book. And where he spake with Jacob at Bethel, there he spake with us, saith Hosea, Chap. 12. 4. And, Whatsoever was written, was written for our learning, saith Paul, Rom. 14. 4.

entries.title: Matthew 15:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
And they are no changelings: For at this day, although they know better, and can [ilegible] the walls of their Synagogues this sentence, Tephillah [ilegible] cheguph belo neshamah, that is, Praier without ([ilegible]. Abbreviat. p. 186.) the intention of the minde, is but as a body without a soul; yet shall not a man any where see lesse intention then in their orisons. The reverence they shew (saith Sr Edwin Sands, who [ilegible] it) is in standing up at times, and the gesture of adoration, in the bowing forward of their bodies. For kneeling they use none (no more do the Grecians) neither stir they their bonnets in their Synagogues to any man: but remain still covered. They come to ([ilegible] Europe.) it with washen hands, and in it they burn lamps to the honour of God: but for any shew of devotion or elevation of spirit, that yet ([ilegible] posset [ilegible], [ilegible] pro [ilegible] quam pro [ilegible]. [ilegible] S [ilegible] epist. 1. [ilegible] 1.) in Jews could I never discern: but they are as reverend in their Synagogues, as Grammer-boyes are at school, when their master is absent. In summe, their holinesse is the very outward work it self, being a brainlesse head, and soullesse body. Thus he.

And honoureth me with their lips] But prayer is not the labour of the lips, but the travel of the heart: the power of a petition is not in the roof of the mouth, but root of the heart. To give way to wilfull distractions, is to commit spirituall whoredom in Gods presence. Is it fit to present the King with an empty cask? or to tell him a tale with our backs towards him? Behold, I am a great King, saith God, and they that stand before him, must look (Eccles. 7. 1.) to their feet, saith Solomon, that they stand upright, and that they offer not an heartlesse sacrifice, for that is the sacrifice of fools, and ever held ominous.

But their heart is farre from me] And so, all they do is puted hypocrisie. God loves truth in the inward parts, Psal. 41. 6. and calls for the heart in all services, as Joseph did for Benjamin, as David did for Michal, Thou shalt not see my face, unlesse thou bring it. In all spirituall Sacrifices we must bring him the fat and the inwards. The deeper and hollower the belly of the lute or viol is, the pleasanter is the sound; the fleeter, the more grating and harsh in our ears. The voice which is made in the mouth is nothing so sweet, as that which cometh from the depth of the brest, Eph. 6. 5. Do the will of God from the heart. But woe be to all carelesse [ilegible], to all loose and ungirt Christians: the Lord will make all the Churches to know that he searcheth the hearts and (Revel. 1. 23.) reyns, and that he will kill with death all such as had rather seem to be good, then seek to be so.

entries.title: Matthew 15:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
For they loose their labour, and which is worse, they commit sinne. Displeasing service is double dishonour, as dissembled sanctity is double iniquity.

Teaching for doctrines the commandments of men] So do Papists. (Host c. 4.) The Pope can do all things that Christ can do, saith Hostiensis. He (Bellar. de pont.) can of [ilegible] make righteousnesse, saith Bellarmine, of [ilegible], (Rom. l. 4.) [ilegible], of nothing, something. His determinations are ipsissimum [ilegible] verbum, the very word of God, saith Hosius. Murders, treasons, thefts, &c. ther's no command of the morall Law, but they can dispence with it; but none of their ceremoniall Law. Let God, say they, look to the breach of his own Law, we will look to ours. Heathen Socrates and Cicero, shall rise up against (Socrat. ap. Xe. nophon.) these Pseudochristians, and condemn them. God, said Socrates, will be worshipped with that kinde of worship only which himself ([ilegible] non superstitione coli [ilegible] pietate.) hath commanded. He will not be worshipped, said Cicero, with superstition, but with piety.

entries.title: Matthew 15:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Pharisees, those [ilegible], [ilegible] they would not be charmed, Christ will lose no more sweet words upon them; but turns them up as desperate with this inscription on their fore heads, Noluerunt [ilegible]; I would have healed these hypocrites, but they would not be healed. Yea, When I would have healed Ephraim, then (to crosse me) their iniquity was discovered, as the leprosie in their fore-heads. And ([ilegible]. 7. 1.) from such uncouncellable and [ilegible] hearers, if a Minister depart, he doth but his duty: the desertion is on their [ilegible], and not on his, The manifestation of the spirit is given to every man to profit withall, 1 Cor. 12. 7.

entries.title: Matthew 15:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Whether with clean or [ilegible] hands, taken meat [ilegible] not the [ilegible] guilty of Gods wrath. What? Not if abused to surfeting and drunkennesse? saith Bellarmine, who is angry with Christ for this doctrine (Ob.) (as making against theirs directly) and therefore seeks to disprove him. We answer for and with Christ: that he speaks here of the moderate use of meats, which is indifferent. As for the abuse of it to [ilegible] and excesse, this is an evil that cometh out of the heart, and defileth the man, as being a flat breach of the law of God, who every where condemns it.

But that which cometh out of the mouth] That is, out of the heart that muck-hill, thorow the mouth, as thorow a dung-port, that defileth a man worse then any jakes can do. Hence sin is called filthinesse, abomination, the vomit of a dog, the devils excrements, &c. The very visible [ilegible] are [ilegible] by it, and must therefore be purged by [ilegible], as those vessels were that held [ilegible] sin-offering. As for the soul, sin sets such engrained stains upon it, as nothing can fetch out, but the bloud of Christ that [ilegible] lamb.

entries.title: Matthew 15:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. why dost thou then thus call the people to thee, and exclude them? It was a commendable charity in the [ilegible], to desire the better information of those that had [ilegible] accused [ilegible], v. 2. and to tender their salvation. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good. Speciosiùs aliquantò injuriae [ilegible] sicijs vincuntur, quam mutni odij pertinacia pensantur, saith a [ilegible]. ([ilegible]. [ilegible] l. 4. cap. 2.)

entries.title: Matthew 15:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: viz. By election, and watered by vocation. These Pharisees were reprobates, designed to detection here, and to destruction hereafter. Therefore as it is no wonder, so it is no matter, though they stumble at the Word, being disobedient, sith hereunto they were appointed, 1 Pet. 2. 8. Let them stumble and fall, and be broken, and snared, and taken, Isa 8. 15. Christ is to reprobates a rock of offence: but such a rock as that, Judg. 6. 21. out of which goeth fire and consumeth them.

entries.title: Matthew 15:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
A dreadfull doom; like that, Hos. 4. 14. I will not punish your daughters, when they commit whoredom, &c. No so great punishment as not to be punished. And vers. 17. of that same Chapter, Ephraim is joyned to idols, let him alone, q. d. He hath made a match with mischief, he shall have his belly-full of it. Never was Jerusalems condition so desperate, as when God said unto her, My fury shall depart from thee, I will be quiet, and no more angry, Ezek. 16. 42. A man is ever and anon medling with his fruit-trees, paring and pruning, &c. but for his oaks, and other trees of the forrest, he lets them alone, till he comes, once for all, with his axe to fell them.

Both shall fall into the ditch] Though the blinde guides fall undermost, and have the worst of it.

entries.title: Matthew 15:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It was no parable, but a plain [ilegible], and easie to be understood, had not they been dull of hearing, and somewhat soured with the Pharisaicall [ilegible] of the necessity of washing hands afore [ilegible]: though for that time, by a singular providence of God, [ilegible] neglected; which both gave [ilegible] to the Pharisees quarrell, and to this question, whereto [ilegible] Saviour maketh a most plain and plenary [ilegible].

entries.title: Matthew 15:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What? Not at these (1 Tim. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) years, and after so long standing? Will ye stand, till ye waxe ([ilegible] adhuc pro [ilegible], at these years; now that you are ut full stature, and in your full vigour?) sour again, and not give your selves wholly to these things, that your profiting may appear to all? Is it not a shame to have no more wit at sixty year old, then at six? to be alwaies learning, yet never [ilegible] to the knowledge of the truth? God expects a proportion of skill and [ilegible] according to the time and means men have had, Heb. 5 12.

entries.title: Matthew 15:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In nature, Animantis cujusque vita est fuga: Life, were it not for the repair by daily [ilegible], would be soon extinguished. Hence it is called, ([ilegible]. 5. 7, 10.) The life of our hand, because maintained by the labour of our [ilegible]. But that which our Saviour here driveth at is, to set forth the ridiculous [ilegible]: of the Pharisees, whiles they placed a kinde of [ilegible] in those things that were evacuated and thrown into ([ilegible] ad Episc. [ilegible]. de [ilegible],) the draught. And do not Papists the very [ilegible]? Qui gustavit ovum trahitur in carcerem, cogiturque de haeresi causam dicere, saith Erasmus. To eat flesh, or but an egg in Lent, is punished with death. Whereas in the year of Christ, 330, Spiridion a godly Bishop in Cyprus, having not what else ready to set before a guest that came to him in the Lent, set him a piece of porke to feed on. And when the stranger made scruple of eating flesh in Lent, saying I am a Christian, and may not do it: Nay therefore thou maist (R m 14) do it said he, because to the pure all things are pure, and the [ilegible] of God consisteth not in meats and drinks, &c.

entries.title: Matthew 15:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That source of sinne, and fountain of folly: for as a fountain casteth forth her waters, so doth the heart of man cast out it's wickednesse, Jer. 6. 7. and if the [ilegible] be a world of wick dnesse, Jam. 2. what is the heart, ([ilegible].) that seminary of sinne, wherein is a [ilegible] as Empedocles saith in Aristotle. In this sea are not only that Leviathan the devil (who there sets up his forts and strong holds, 2 Cor. 10. 4. and doth entrench and incage himself) but creeping things innumerable, Psal. 104. 26. making that which should be the Temple of God a den of theeves, a pallace of pride, a slaughter-house of malice, a [ilegible]-house of [ilegible], a raging sea of sinne, Isa. 57. 20. a little hell of black and [ilegible] imaginations. The [ilegible] man [ilegible] rotting in the grave of corruption, wrapt up in the winding-sheet of hardnesse of heart, and blindenesse of minde; and ([ilegible] a [ilegible] crawleth with wormes) swarming with those [ilegible] lusts, that were able to poison up an honest heart.

entries.title: Matthew 15:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These are the first and immediate issue of the sinfull soul: words and ([ilegible].) deeds, Borborology and enormity follow in their order. And I dare be bold to say (saith a reverend Divine) that though the act contract the guilt, because the lust is then [ilegible] up to an height, so that it is come to an absolute will in execution, yet the act of adultery and murther is not so abhominable in Gods [ilegible], as the [ilegible] of the spirit: for it is the spirit that he mainly looks to, &c. Think not then that thought is free, for as inward bleeding will kill, so [ilegible] concupiscence, whatever the Papists say in favour of it, [ilegible] a condition of nature: and [ilegible] flow most of their most [ilegible] opinions, as justification by works, state of perfection, [ilegible], [ilegible], &c.

entries.title: Matthew 15:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Make him a [ilegible] in Gods sight, his heart being a filthy [ilegible] of all [ilegible] vices, his life a long chain of sinfull actions, a very continued web of wickednesse. And whereas Repentance is the souls vomit, and Confession the spunge that wipes out all the blots and blurres of our lives, that cunning manslayer holds the lips elose that the heart may not disburden it self by so ([ilegible].) wholesome evacuation, and doth what he can to hinder the birth of Repentance, that fair and happy daughter of an uggly and odious (De Pompeio Romani ap. [ilegible]. in vita Hist. of holy War.) mother, sinne.

entries.title: Matthew 15:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That royall exchange of the world, as one calleth it. Hither retired our Saviour, as tired out with the Jews perversenesse. And here it's like he did much good, according to that was prophesied, Isa. 23. 18. Sure it is, that whereas here he would have hid himself, he could not, for the woman of Canaan came and fell at his feet as a suppliant for her daughter. (Mark 7. 24. [ilegible], a tergo [ilegible].)

entries.title: Matthew 15:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
One coppy hath it, And cryed behinde him: which implies either that Christ had turned his back upon her, seeing her now coming towards him; or [ilegible] that she was abashed to come into his presence, as being of an accurfed kindred, devoted to destruction.

Have mercy upon me, ô Lord] She acknowledged her own sinne in her daughters sufferings. So did that other good woman, 1 King. 17. 18. Her son was dead, her sinne was called to remembrance. And so must we see our selves beaten on our sick childrens (2 [ilegible]. 12. 16.) backs, as David did, and be humbled, labouring to mend by education, what we have marred by propagation.

Thou son of David] Thou that wast thy self born of a woman, pity a woman: thou that hast the bowels of a man in thee, hide not thine eies from thine own flesh.

My daughter is grievously vexed with a devil] The devil doth his worst to her, therefore help. Misery makes men eloquent, beyond truth many times: But surely this womans case was very dolefull. It was her daughter, dear to her as her own (Lambin in Menech Plauti Act.) soul. Filia quasi [ilegible]. The Greeks call children [ilegible] the Latines Chara. And those at Rome, that prayd and sacrificed whole daies that their children might be superstites long-lived, these were (1 [ilegible]. 1.) first called superstitious persons. Quod nomen patuit poste à [ilegible], (Domi domitus [ilegible].) saith Cieero. The word aftsrwards came to be of larger signification. This (perhaps only) daughter, was vexed and grievously (De nat. [ilegible].) vexed, and that of a devil: who ever busie enough to do mischeif, yet then cheifly [ilegible] him to set up his kingdome, when Christ came to pull it down. And as he oncestrove with Michael about a dead mans body, but it was that he might thereby set up himself in living mens souls: So he still seeks to possesse himself of our bodies, that thereby he may the better winde and work himself into our hearts.

entries.title: Matthew 15:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Tacet ore, sed loquitur ei spiritu, ut fortiùs clamet, saith an interpreter. Christ answereth her not with his mouth, but speaketh unto her by that sweet and secret voice of his spirit, to cry louder. No man prayes heartily but he hath so much comfort at least, that he will come again to God, who secretly supports his suppliants, and by ([ilegible].) that peace unconceivable guards their hearts and mindes that they (Philip 4. 7.) pray and faint not.

Send her away, for she cries] Men may be tired out with uncessant suites, as the unjust Judge was, and as these Disciples were weary to hear the poor womans outcries, repeating the same request over and over: Give her therefore, say they, either an almes or an answer; that she may be silenced and we eased. But it is otherwise with God, the oftener we come to him the better welcome: the louder we cry, the sooner we are heard: and the often repetition of the self-same petition, till we put the Lord out of countenance, put him (as you would say) to the blush, and even [ilegible] a blot in [ilegible] face, as the Greek word signifies, Luk 18. 5. ([ilegible]) this is the best melody we can [ilegible] him. He looks out of the casements of heaven on purpose to hear it.

entries.title: Matthew 15:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He was properly the Apostle of the Circumcision, Rom. 15. 8. Heb. 3. 1. till the wall of partition was broken down by his resurrection. Then the [ilegible] rent, and it was open-tide. Then he became light to lighten the Gentiles, as well as he was the glory of his people Israel.

entries.title: Matthew 15:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
She will not be said nay, or set down, either with silence or sad answers; but, like another Gorgonia, she threatens heaven, and is (as her brother ([ilegible].) speaks of her) modestly impudent and invincible. She will believe, as a man may say with reverence, whether Christ will or no. And to bring her to this it was, that he so long held her off, for, [ilegible] dilata crescunt: at [ilegible] data, vilescunt. Minnah, that light meat, was but lightly set by, because lightly come by. But they that earn it before they eat it, and that know how they come by that they [ilegible], will set an high price upon it, and know how and why they part with it.

Lord, help me] Few words, but very forcible. When thou (Eccles. 5. 1.) comest before God, let thy words [ilegible] few, saith Solomon. This St Peter calls to be sober [ilegible] prayer, [ilegible] Pet. 4 7. without trifling, (Orationis [ilegible] [ilegible] in loc.) or vain babling, which the wise man calls the sacrifice of fools. The Baalites prayer was not more tedious, then Eliah's short, and yet more pithy then short: charging God with the care of his covenant, truth, glory, &c. It was Eliah that praid loud and long, though in few words, yet very effectuall. Fratres AEgyptiaci brevissimis & raptìm jaculatis orationibus uti voluerunt ([ilegible] Augustine) ne per moras evanesceret & habetaretur intentio. Those ancient Christians of Egypt were very brief in [ilegible] prayers.

Help me] The word properly signifieth to run at ones cry that ([ilegible] [ilegible] [ilegible] al [ilegible] [ilegible]. [ilegible] [ilegible]. [ilegible].) calls for help, as the tender mother doth to her hungry child, when he sets up his note, and cries lustily.

entries.title: Matthew 15:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To whelps, saith St Mark, So he calls her, Bitch, her daughter, whelp. This might have easily [ilegible] and discouraged her. But she was that well resolved Christian, whose part Luther saith it is to believe things invisible, to [ilegible] for things deferred, and to love God when he shews himself most angry with him, and most opposite to him. Our Saviour was no sooner gon from this Canaanitesse but he heals the ([ilegible], [ilegible] dilata, & a [ilegible] Deu [ilegible] contrarium Luth. [ilegible]. 30. 18.) [ilegible] and dumb man (though far weaker in faith then her) at first word, Mark. 7. 33. and vers. 30 of this chapter the Galileans no sooner laid then sick and lame friends at [ilegible] feet, but he cured them [ilegible] any more a do. He is a God of judgement, and knowes how and when to deal forth his favours. He laies heaviest [ilegible] on the strongest backs, and proportions our afflictions to our [ilegible], holding us off for deliverance, till [ilegible] finds us [ilegible] for it: and giving us hearts to wait, and want it till his time is come.

entries.title: Matthew 15:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
[ilegible] [ilegible]. This is particula assentientis & obsecrantis. How strangely doth God enable and enlarge his weak people many times in prayer? they are carried beyond themselves in a wonderfull manner, and though otherwise rude in speech and [ilegible], yet then they have words at will, far above naturall apprehension, and such as they are not able to repeat again: being for the time, lost in the endlesse maze of spirituall ravishments, and ascending, with the Church, in those pillars of incense, out of this wildernesse of the World. ([ilegible]. 5. 6.)

Yet the dogs eat of the crumbs] Loe she picks an argument of speeding out of a repulse; she gathereth one contrary out of another by the force of her faith. See the like, Deut. 32. 36. 2 King. 14. 26. Going into captivitie was a signe of the Israelites returning out of captivitie. Be it that I am a dog saith this brave woman, yet some crumbs of comfort, Lord. Dogs, though they may not eat the childrens meat (if they offer to do it, they are shut out of doors) yet if children full-fed crumble their meat, and make wast of it, as they will, and as the Jews now do, may not the Gentile-dogs lick up those leavings? Thus she reasons it, and thus she makes use of any thing she can lay hold of, whereby she may hope the better to prevail. Those that are hunger-starved are glad to feed upon hedge-fruit, and will make hard shift rather then perish. So, faithfull hearers are not delicate, but can suffer an exhortation, bear a reproof, yea suck hony, with the bee, out (Heb. 13.) of bitter thime.

entries.title: Matthew 15:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Our Saviour had both reproached and repulsed her. Now he both graceth and gratifieth her; grants her request and more, together with an high commendation of her heroicall [ilegible], which is here found [ilegible] to praise and honour and glory, 1 Pet. 1. 7.

entries.title: Matthew 15:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Where though he had lately been tired out, yet he'l try again. Ministers must have patience with a perverse people, not resolving, as Ieremy once in a pelt, to speak no more to them in the name of the Lord, but proving if at any time God will give them repentance to the acknowleging of the truth, &c. 2 Tim. 2. 25. I beseech you (said Mr Bradford to one with whom he had taken great pains, but to no great purpose) I pray you, I desire you, I crave at your hands with all my very heart; I ask of you with hand, pen, tongue, ([ilegible]. and [ilegible].) and minde, in Christ, for Christ, through Christ, for his name, blood, mercy, power and truths sake, my most entirely beloved, that you admit no doubting of Gods finall mercies toward you, howsoever you feel your self, &c. Of this good Martyr it is said, that in travelling with his own heart he would never give over till he had made somewhat of it, as in confession, till his heart melted, in seeking pardon till quieted, in begging grace, till warmed (Aug de [ilegible]: Christ: & in, [ilegible].) and quickened: so in dealing with others he practised that which St Austin perswadeth every preacher to do, so long to beat upon and repeat the same point, till by the countenance, but especially by the conversation of his hearers, he perceive that they resent and rellish it. Knowing the terrour of the Lord, saith Paul, [ilegible] perswade men; we give them not over till we have prevailed (2 Cor. [ilegible] 1.) with them and subdued them, though never so knotty and knorly.

And went up into a mountain] Either to pray, or to preach, or to rest and repose himself; but that would not be: for great multitudes resorted to him. The Sun set on high cannot be hid, no more can Christ in the mount.

entries.title: Matthew 15:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All these infirmities are fruits of sin (which hath made the world an Occumeniall Hospitall) and accidents of life; for that which (Cu [ilegible] contingere quod [ilegible] quam contigit. [ilegible]. [ilegible] plures sunt [ilegible] positivae. Gerson.) befalleth any man, may befall every man. The privative favours that God shews us here (saith Gerson,) are more then the positive: meaning by privative, Gods preserving us from manifold mischiefs and miseries by his manutension, They that are got to heaven are out of the gunshot: for there's no more sicknesse, nor sorrow, no crying, nor pain, for the former things are passed, Revel. 21. 4. All corruptions, temptations, afflictions, which stand, some above us, some about us (as the insulting Philistims about blinde Sampson) shall end with the same blow, fall with the same clap with our selves. At Stratford bow were two Martyrs burned at one stake (in the dayes of Q. Mary) Hugh Laverock an old lame man, and Iohn A Price a blinde man. At their death, Hugh, after he was chained, casting away his crutch, and comforting the other, he said to him, Be of good comfort my brother, for my Lord of [ilegible] is our good Physitian: he will heal us shortly, thee of thy (Act. and Mon. [ilegible] 1733.) [ilegible], and me of my lamenesse. And so patiently they suffered.

entries.title: Matthew 15:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They saw God in those miraculous cures, and gave him his due praise. He is content that we should have the comfort of his benefits, so he may [ilegible] the glory of them; that's all the rent and return he looks for. All the [ilegible] Christ required for his cures was, Go and tell what God [ilegible] for thee, Go shew thy self to the Priest and offer, &c. But we, insteed of being temples of Gods praise, become many times graves of his benefits. This made good David so oft to put the thorn to his breast, Psal. 103. 1,2,3. and King Alphonsus not so much to wonder at his Courtiers ingratitude to him, as at his own to God.

entries.title: Matthew 15:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
My bowels yearn towards them. Neither is he [ilegible] loving now that he is in heaven, towards his poor pennilesse [ilegible] people on earth: but when they are hardest put to't, and haply have not a crosse to blesse themselves with, as the proverb is, he so graciously provides, that though the young lions (or the strong ones, as the Septuagint ([ilegible]. 34 10.) have it) doe lack and suffer hunger, yet they that seek the Lord want nothing that's good for them. Aaron though he might not bewail the death of his two sons, Lev. 10. because he was High-priest, yet his bowels of fatherly affection towards them, could not be restrained. Christ retaineth still compassion, Heb. 45. ([ilegible] 9. 5.) though free from personall passion: and, though freed from feeling, ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) hath [ilegible] yet a fellow-feeling. Manet compassio etiam cum impassibilitate, saith Bernard.

Because they continue with me now three dayes] The Lord takes punctuall and particular notice of all circumstances, how far they came, how long they had been there, how little able they were to hold out fasting to their own homes, &c. And so he doth still, recount how many years, daies, hours we have spent with him: what straits, [ilegible], hears, colds, dangers, difficulties we have [ilegible] with and passed thorow; all is exactly registred in his book of remembrance: I know thy work, and thy [ilegible], saith he, ([ilegible] 2. 19.) Rev. 2. Men take much pains many times, and none regard it, reward it. But Christ takes notice, not of his peoples works only, but of their labour in doing them, that he may [ilegible] recompence their labour of love, their losse of goods, &c. the godly shall know in themselves, not only in others, in books &c. that they have a better, and an enduring substance, Heb. 10. 34.

entries.title: Matthew 15:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See their stupidity ([ilegible] ut [ilegible], [ilegible].) and diffidence, yet still budging and [ilegible] out, upon all occasions. What a life hath Christ with the best of us, ere he can bring ([ilegible]. [ilegible]) us to any thing? Corruption will have some slurts, some out-bursts. [ilegible] cleaves to us more [ilegible] then this evil heart of unbelief: like a fretting leprosie in our cottages of clay, though the walls be well scraped, yet it will never utterly out, till the house be demolished.

entries.title: Matthew 15:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Before, he had fed five thousand with fewer loaves. God can as easily maintain us with a little, as with more; witnesse Daniels pulie, and Eliah's cake on the coals, and cruse of water; Luthers herring, and Iunius his ([ilegible]. 19. 6.) one egge a day, when means was short with him, by reason of the civil wars in France, so that he could not hear from his friends. It is not by bread only that man liveth, but by the word of Gods (Melch. Adam. in vita Lutheri. Iun. in vita sua.) blessing, that maketh it nourishable. As if he break the staffe of bread, that is, his own blessing, which is the staffe whereon bread (that staffe of life) leaneth, it can neither feed nor fill, make men neither fuller, nor fatter.

entries.title: Matthew 15:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He intended them not only a running-banquet, a slightcome-off, but a full feast, a good meal, and therefore bad them sit down, and feed their fill. It was indeed on the bare ground that they sate: but so doe the greatest (Turk. Hist. fol. 713.) Lords in Turky at this day: they sit at meat, with their legs gathered under them, flat upon the ground; and their chear, when they feast most sumptuously, is only rice and mutton, with fair water out of the river.

entries.title: Matthew 15:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So confuting their unbelief, and confirming their faith for the future. And the like he doth for us every time we receive the Sacrament of his Supper. He bespeaks us there, as he did peremptory Thomas, Joh. 20. 27.

And the Disciples to the multitude] This is Christs course to this day: by the hands of his faithfull Ministers, to deal forth his favours, to give his holy Spirit (which is, to give all good things, Matth. 7. 11. with Luk. 11. 13.) by the preaching of faith. This (Num. 11. 9.) Manna comes down from heaven in the dews of the Ministry. If (1 Pet. 1. 22.) our eyes see not our teachers, we cannot expect to hear the voice behinde us, Isa. 30. 20.

entries.title: Matthew 15:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
They did eat to ([ilegible], Hoc proprie [ilegible] de armentis. [ilegible] [ilegible] [ilegible] gramen aut pabulum. Bez[ilegible].) saturity, as men use to doe at feasts, where the tables seem to sweat with variety. The Greek word here is, in its proper signification, used of fatting cattle, that have grasse up to the eyes, such as is that in some parts of Ireland, where they are forced to drive out their cattle sometimes from the pastures into the commons, lest they should surfet and spoil themselves.

Seven baskets full] These baskets were bigger and of larger capacity then those coffins. Matth. 14. 20. we read of Paul let ([ilegible].) down by the wall in a basket. Acts 9. 20. It was such a vessel then, that a man might sit in it: as the former may seem to have been no larger then a pye or pasty, the outside whereof, from the Greeks, we call a coffin.

entries.title: Matthew 15:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Chap. 14 21. Herein was the majesty of the miracle, that there was no proportion between the men, and the meat.

entries.title: Matthew 15:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not without a blessing, and a great deal of good counsell. Labour not for the meat that perisheth &c. Amend your lives, for the Kingdom of heaven is come home to you: Now that you have eaten and are full, beware that you forget not the Lord your God, &c. Be not as children, with whom eaten bread is soon forgotten. This was wholesome (Deut. 8, 10, 11.) counsel, and far better then their good chear; for this would stick by them. Deal we so by our guests.

And came into the coasts of Magdala.] This is held to be Mary Magdalens country, better known by her then she was by it, as the Island of Co was by Hippocrates, and Hippo by Austin.

entries.title: Matthew 16:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
CAme forth, saith S. Marke, to wit out of the coasts of Magdala, ([ilegible]) so soon as ever our Saviour arrived there, to quarr[ilegible]ll him, and keep him from doing good. So active are the devils instruments to hinder the Kingdom of God, and the good of souls. Truth never wants an adversary; she goes seldom without a scratcht face, as the Proverbe is. The Pharisees and Sadduces, though at deadly difference betwixt themselves, yet can easily combine against Christ. So at this day, the Priests disparage the Jesuits, the Jesuits the Priests, the Priests again the Monks, the Monks the Friers, but they can all conspire against Protestants, whom they jointly persecute. Doggs though they fight never so fierce, and mutually entertear one another; yet, if a hare run by, they give over, and run after her. Martial makes mention of a hare on the Sicilian shore, that having hardly escaped the hounds that hunted her, was devoured by a sea dog; whereupon he brings her in thus complaining; In me omnis terraeque aviumque marisque rapina est: (Martial. Epigram) For sitan & coeli, si canis astra tenet.

Tempting, desired him] Or questioned him to and fro, sifted ([ilegible], [ilegible].) him by interrogatories, pretending to be his friends, and to seek satisfaction only. All this savours strongly of putid hypocrisie, quae ipsis domestica [ilegible] virtus, as one saith of them. Socinus did (Aretius.) in like sort set upon Zanchius. He was, saith Zanchius, a learned (Homo suit plenus diver sarum [ilegible], quas tamen [ilegible] nisi [ilegible] causâ, & [ilegible] quasi [ilegible] doceri. Zanch. [ilegible]. ad [ilegible] operi suo de [ilegible]. [ilegible]. ipsis. q. solu.) man, and of unblameable conversation, but full of heresies, which yet he never propounded to me otherwise then by way of question; as seeming desirous to be better informed. By this subtle means, he drew away many, and sought to work upon Zanchius, as did also Matthaeus Gribaldus and some such others. But when they could not prevail, they brake friendship with him, and he with them, for the which he praiseth God from the bottom of his heart.

Shew them a signe] Them, by all means, as more worshipfull men then the multidude, such as might merit an extraordinary signe. See here their Satanicall arrogance. So Herod would see our Saviour, that he might see a signe from him. He looked upon him no otherwise then upon some common juggler, that would sure shew him his best tricks. Thus these hypocrites here would gladly be gratified, but they were deceived.

entries.title: Matthew 16:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Are you so weather-wise (which yet is not your profession?) are ye so skilfull in nature, and yet so ignorant of scripture, as not to know, that now is the time for the Messias, to come, and that I am He? surely you are either notorious sots, or deep dissemblers, or both, in seeming so curiously to search after the truth, which yet you [ilegible] care to know, nor obey.

entries.title: Matthew 16:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The men of Issachar were in great account with David, because they had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to doe, 1 Chron. 12. 32. A prudent man foreseeth an evil, and hideth himself, Prov. 22. 3. He foreseeth it; not by divination, or starregazing, but by a judicious collection and connection of causes and [ilegible]: as, if God be the same that ever, as holy, just, powerfull, &c. If sin be the same that ever, as foul, loathsome, pernicious, &c. then such and such events will follow upon such and such [ilegible]. As God hath given us signes and fore-tokens of a tempest, so he hath also of an ensuing judgement, and blames those that take not notice thereof; sending them to school to the stork and swallow, Jer 87. If Elias see but a cloud as a hand, arising from Carmel, he can tell that a great store of rain will follow, that the whole heaven will anon be covered. Finer tempers are [ilegible] sensible of change of weather. Moses, as more acquainted with God, spies his wrath at first setting out: so might we have done ere it came to this, and have redeemed a great part of our present sorrows, had we had our eyes in our heads, Eccles. 2. 14 had we not been of those wilfull ones, who seek straws to put out their eyes withall, as Bernard hath it, or that wink for the nonce, saith [ilegible] (Qui [ilegible] quaerunt unde oculos [ilegible] Bern.) Martyr, that they may not see, when some unsavoury potion is ministred unto them.

entries.title: Matthew 16:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the Notes ([ilegible].) on Chap. 12. 39. The same wedge [ilegible], the same knot. They shall have no new answer from Christ, till they have made [ilegible] use of the old: Let them return to thee, not thou to them, Jer. 15. 19.

And [ilegible] left them, and departed] Because he saw his sweet words were even spilt upon them. Frustrà lavantur AEthiopes, & certatur cum hypocritis: none are more obstinate and obdurate.

entries.title: Matthew 16:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As wholly transported with fervour in following Christ the bread of life. This is the fault of but a few now-adayes: worldly cares eat up heavenly desires, as the lean kine in Pharoahs dream, did the fat.

entries.title: Matthew 16:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Or take knowledge ([ilegible] [ilegible] est [ilegible] [ilegible].) of, and then take heed of false doctrine; which is fitly called leaven, because it sowreth, swelleth, spreadeth, corrupteth the whole lump, and all this secretly, slily, easily, suddenly; neither can our eyes discern it from dowe by the colour, but only our pallate by the tast. Now the [ilegible] trieth words, as the mouth trieth meat, Job 343. Try all things before you trust any thing. Those that sow [ilegible] doctrine, are somewhere in the Acts called [ilegible], pests, (Acts 24. 5.) botches, for their danger of infection: some can carry their collusion so cleanly, that if possible the very elect might be deceived; like serpents, they can sting without hissing; like cur-doggs, suck your bloud without biting. Nota est Arry [ilegible], saith one, quâ ([ilegible] ponentes [ilegible] [ilegible].) [ilegible] de fide Ni [ilegible] elusit examen, by the cogging of a dye, by the adding of one Iota, they corrupted the sense of the (Habuerunt [ilegible] quo [ilegible] quam [ilegible]. [ilegible].) whole Synod. The Valentinians had a trick to perswade before they taught. The ancient Antiirinitarians set forth a base book of their doctrines under [ilegible] name, and sold it dog-cheap, that men might the sooner [ilegible] it, and be led by it, as Ruffinus complains. Take heed and beware of such: ye are not ignorant of their wiles.

Of the Pharisees, and of the Sadduces.] [ilegible], (Erasm. [ilegible].) Never a barrel better herring. Howbeit the Sadduces affected, by their very name, to be held the only just men; haply (Joseph. lib. 17. cap 3. & 18. cap. 1.) because they held, that all the reward that righteous men are to look for, is here in this world. The occasion of this [ilegible] is said to be this. When Antigonus taught, that we must not serve God for wages, his scholars understood him, as if he had utterly denied all (Godwin. [ilegible].) future rewards or recompence attending a godly life: and thence framed their heresie, denying the Resurrection, world to come, Angels, devils, and lived as Epicures and Libertines.

entries.title: Matthew 16:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Oh the dullnesse that is in the best to receive or retain heavenly mysteries! Surely, as Owls see best by night, and are blinde by day: so in deeds of darknesse we are sharpsighted, wise to doe evil; but in spirituals, we are blinder then beetles, our wits serve us not, we are singularly [ilegible] and stubborn.

entries.title: Matthew 16:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Fides famem non formidat. It was want of faith that made them fear they should perish in the wildernesse for lack of bread: God was better to them then their fears. He makes the best living of it, that lives by faith: Feed on faith: So Tremellius reads that, Psal. 37. 3.

Why reason ye amongst your selves?] [ilegible] likely laid the ([ilegible]; Disserere [ilegible], ac [ilegible] interse disceptare.) fault of forgetfullnesse one upon another: but none found fault with himself for his unbelief, and carnall reasoning.

entries.title: Matthew 16:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Tantum didicimus, quantum [ilegible]. So much we learn as we remember. Our memories (Discere, voluit Socrates nihil aliud esse [ilegible] recordari. Cic. Tusc. [ilegible].) are naturally like hour-glasses, no sooner filled with good instructions and experiments, then running out again. It must be our prayer to God, that he would put his finger upon the hole, and so make our memories like the pot of Mannah, preserving holy truths in the Ark of the soul.

entries.title: Matthew 16:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Learn to lay up experiences. (D. Sibbs.) If we were well read in the story of our own lives (saith a Reverent man) we might have a Divinity of our own. The Philosopher saith, that experience is multiplex memoria, because, of the [ilegible] of the same thing often done, ariseth experience, which should be the nurse of confidence.

entries.title: Matthew 16:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ignorance under means is a blushfull sin. The Scripture calls such, Horses, Asses, [ilegible], and sends them to school to unreasonable creatures.

entries.title: Matthew 16:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This chiding then was well bestowed. So was that, Luk. 24, [ilegible]. upon the two [ilegible] going to Emaus, and that upon the Virgin Mary, Joh. 2. 5. she laid her hand upon her mouth and replied not. And that upon the Corinthians for conniving at the incestuous [ilegible], and that upon the Laodiceans, Rev. 3. 14. for Eusebius telleth us, that in his time it continued to be a flourishing Church. It is said of [ilegible], (In [ilegible] [ilegible].) that he took not content in any thing so much, as in a plain and faithfull reproof from his friend. It is a commendation to [ilegible] the words of exhortation, Heb. 13.

entries.title: Matthew 16:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This Question Christ asked, not as tickled with ambition to hear his own commendation ([ilegible] Xenopbon.) (which yet is held and said to be the only sweet hearing) but as taking occasion to make way for their Christian confession, and likewise for their further information.

The sonne of man am?] So he was called. 1. Because a true man. 2. Because he passed for no more then an ordinary man. How can this man give us his flesh to [ilegible]? Joh. 6. 3. Because as man born of a woman, he was of few daies and full of trouble: yea, he was the man that had seen affliction by the rod of Gods wrath.

entries.title: Matthew 16:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His body they saw was not Johns, but they held then (and the Jews at this day hold) the Pythagorean transanimation, or passing of souls out of one body into another. So, because they received not the love of the truth, God gave them up to the efficacy of errour, even the better sort of them: for there were that held ([ilegible] 2. 11.) Christ neither the Baptist, nor Elias, but a drunkard, a demoniack, &c. Who now can think to escape variety of censures? And why should any stumble at the diversity of opinions touching Christ and his kingdom?

entries.title: Matthew 16:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. It behoveth you to say something, that is, better to the purpose, [ilegible] the vulgar saith and censureth. God will take that of some that he will not of others. Christ would not have his to stand doubtfull, and to [ilegible] to nothing certainly: to be in religion as idle beggars are in their way, ready to go which way soever the staff [ilegible]: but to strive to a plerophory, a full assurance of knowledge, a certainty, as Luke hath it, chap. 1. 4. and to be [ilegible] perswaded, vers. 1. A conjecturall confidence, a generall faith, the Colliers faith, [ilegible] they call it, sufficeth not, To believe as the Church believes, &c. And yet Thomas Aquinas, that great Schoolman had no better a faith to support him at the last hour of his life: nor could he have any rest within, till he had taken up the Bible, and clipping it in his arms, said, Lord, I believe all that is written in this holy book.

entries.title: Matthew 16:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
As the mouth of the company, and one that being, haply, [ilegible], and surely bolder then the rest, spake thus for them. But what a [ilegible] mouth of blasphemy opened those two Popes (Peters pretended successours) Leo (Petrum in consortium individuae [ilegible] assumptum [ilegible] ârunt, Renius) the first, and Nicolas the third, that boasted, that Peter was taken into fellowship of the individuall Trinity? Neither can that be excused that Hierom commenteth on the former verses (Whom [ilegible] say that I am? But whom say [ilegible] that I am?) that our Saviour there purposely opposeth his Disciples to men, to intimate that they were something more then men. This is some thing like that Note of a Latine Postiller upon Exo. 30. 31. where, because it is said, vers. 32. Upon mans flesh the holy ointment shall not be poured, thou [ilegible] anoint Aaron and his sonnes therewith, thence infers, that Priests are Angels, and have not humane flesh. These were humane [ilegible], and savoured as little of Gods meaning, as that unsavoury speech of Peter, v. 22. of this Chapter, for the which he [ilegible], Get thee behinde me, Satan: thou savourest not, &c.

Verse Thou art Christ the Sonne of the living God] A short ([ilegible]. Singulae [ilegible] suos [ilegible] [ilegible] adjectos. Arct.) confession, but such as in few, containeth whatsoever we believe concerning the person and osfice of Christ, Brevis & longa planeque aurea est baec confessio. [ilegible] we say of it, as St Bartholomew (quoted by Dionysius) did of the Doctrine of Divinity, that it is, [ilegible], Little and yet large.

entries.title: Matthew 16:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These and the following words of our Saviour to Peter, were meant to all the Apostles also, Joh. 20. 22, 23. Christ took his beginning of one, to teach unity in his Church, in the confession of faith. Note this against the Papists, who miserably wrest, and [ilegible] this text, to the proving of the [ilegible] Monarchy. Gregory the great, though he stiled himself a servant of Gods servants, and detested the Pope of Censtantinople for arrogating the title of [ilegible], during the raign of Mauritius: yet when he was [ilegible], and succeeded by the traitour Phocas, he ceased not to flatter the same Phocas, to commend unto him the care of the Church of Rome, and to exhort ([ilegible]. [ilegible], [ilegible]. [ilegible].) him to remember this saying of our Saviour, Thou art Peter, &c. and for no other end, then that he might extend his power by the favour of the parricide.

entries.title: Matthew 16:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
i. e. Thou art a living stone in the spirituall Temple, like as `Peter saith all other Christians are, 1 Pet. 2. 5. And here Christ tels Peter why at first he gave him that name.

Upon this Rock] That is, upon this thy Rocky, thy solid and substantiall confession of me. Austin saith, the rock is Christ, not ([ilegible] verb. Dem. Serm 13.) Peter, But this, saith [ilegible], is, humanus lapsus in Augustino. ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. 6. c. 3.) So the Schoolmen say, that St Austin stood so much for grace, that [ilegible] yeelded too little to free-will. But it was a true saying of learned D. Whitakers in his answer to Campian, Patres in [ilegible] sunt nostri, in multis [ilegible], in minimis vestri.

I will build my Church] Christ cals not the Church [ilegible], or ([ilegible], [ilegible], [ilegible] populo age. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) [ilegible], which is properly a convention of Lords and Statesmen, [ilegible] [ilegible], which is an Assembly of the common people, even those of the lower rank and condition according to that 1 Cor. 1. 26. and Luk. 1. 48. he hath regarded the low estate of his [ilegible]-[ilegible].

And the gates of hell, &c.] That is, all the power and policy of hell combined. The devil lendeth his instruments, the Churches [ilegible], his seven heads to plot, and his ten horns to push. Craft and cruelty go together in them, as the Asp never wanders alone: and as the Scripture speaks of those birds of prey, Isa. 34. 16. None of them wants his mate. But yet all this shall not prevail: the devil may shake his chain at the Saints, not set his [ilegible] in them. For why? they stand upon a rock that is higher then they, so that the floods of [ilegible] and oppositions cannot come so much as at their feet: or if they reach to the heel, yet they come not at the head, or if they should dash higher upon them, yet they break themselves.

Shall not prevail against it] No, though the devil should discharge at the Church his [ilegible] ordinance: say they were as big ([ilegible] vally of [ilegible]. 127.) as those two cast by Alphonsus Duke of Ferrara, the one whereof he called the earthquake, and the other Grandiabolo, or the great devil.

Shall not prevail against it] Whether may the Catholike Church erre in fundamentals? ([ilegible].)

Shall not prevail against it] It is answered, that [ilegible] the [ilegible] Church of Christ, (Ans.) taken for his mysticall to [ilegible] upon earth, and complete number of h select, cannot erre in matters fundamentall, yet the externall (D. [ilegible].) visible part of the Church may erre, because the truth of God may be locked up within the hearts of such a company, as in competition of suffrages, cannot make a greater part in a generall Councel: so that the sentence decreed therein, may be a fundamentall errour.

entries.title: Matthew 16:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: i. e. I will make thee and all my Ministers stewards in my hous; 1 Cor. 4. 1. such as Obadiah was in Ahabs house, as Eliakim in Hezekiahs, upon whose shoulder God laid the key of the house of David, so that he opened and none shut, and shut and none opened, Isa. 22. 22. Now let a man so think of us Ministers, how mean soever, and we shall not want for respect.

entries.title: Matthew 16:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: viz. Till the due time. Every thing is beautifull in its season, saith Solomon. Taciturnity in (Eccles. 3.) some cases is a vertue, as here. The Disciples might preach that Christ the Son of David was come to save the world: though they might not particularly point himout, as the Son of the living God: which when Pilate himself heard, he was afraid, saith the text, and sought to deliver him.

entries.title: Matthew 16:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He must, necessitate non simplici, sed ex supposito. It being supposed that God had decreed this way (and no other) to glorifie himself in mans salvation by the death of his dear Son (wherein the naked bowels of his [ilegible] were laid open to us, as in an anatomy) it was necessary that Christ should be killed and raised again at the third day, Voluntu Dei, necessitas rei.

And be killed and raised again] That we might live and raign with him for ever, who else had been killed with death, as the [ilegible] is, Rev. 2. 23. that is, had come under the [ilegible] of the second death. David wished he might have died for Absolom, such was his love to him. Arsinoe interposed her self between the [ilegible] weapons, sent by [ilegible] her brother, to kill her children. The [ilegible] not only feeds her young with her own bloud, but with invincible constancy abides the flames of fire for their preservation. Christ is that good shepherd, who gave his life for his [ilegible]. He is that true Pellican, who saw the wrath of God burning about his young ones, and cast himself into the midst thereof, that he might quench it. He was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification, which began in his death, but (Rom. 4 25.) was perfected by his resurrection.

entries.title: Matthew 16:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Took him by the hand, & led him apart, as we do those we are most [ilegible] with, in great courtesy and secrecy, to impart to them things of greatest importance. Peter was strongly possest with a fond conceit of an earthly kingdom; and as Joseph dreamt of his preferment, but not at all of his imprisonment: so neither could Peter think or hear of Christs being killed, whom he had even now confessed to be the Christ, the son of the living God. See here how easily we slide, by the deceitfulnesse of our hearts, from the mean to the extream. Peter having made a notable profession of his faith, and being therefore much commended by Christ, presently takes occasion to fall from the true holinesse of faith, to the [ilegible] of presumption, in advising his Master to decline the crosse.

And began to rebuke him, saying] No, he did not rebuke him, saith Maldonat the Jesuite, but friendly counselled him only, as (Non tantum significat reprebend re & increpare, sed etiā [ilegible] & interdicere.) if [ilegible] were not to chide and charge, as masters do their servants, even with threatnings and menaces. But these patrons of Peter (as they pretend) will not abide that he should be blamed for any thing. Baronius blusheth not to say (and so to put the lie upon the holy Ghost himself) that Paul was out in reproving (Gerh. Baron. Annal. Sands his Rel. of West. Relig.) Peter, Gal. 2. 14. and that it had been better manners for him to have held his tongue. Others of them have blasphemously censured S. Paul in their Sermons, as a hot-headed person, of whose assertions no great [ilegible] was to be made by the sober-[ilegible] and that he was not secure of his preaching, [ilegible] by conference with S. Peter, neither durst he publish his Epistles, till S. Peter had allowed them.

entries.title: Matthew 16:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Come behinde as a [ilegible] ciple, go not before me as a teacher: understand thy distance, and hold thee to thy duty, by moving in thine own sphear; that [ilegible] be not thus [ilegible] eccentrick, another Satan, who sets thee a work thus to tempt me, as he once did Eve to seduce Adam: here Maldonat is hard put to't, to save [ilegible] blamelesse, and saith, that, Get thee behinde me is an Hebrew phrase, and imports no more then Follow me. But when he comes to consider that Christ calls him Satan, and that it would not be [ilegible] that Christ should bid Satan follow him, he is [ilegible] to confesse that it is the speech of one that bids another be packing out of his presence with indignation, like that of Christ to the tempter, Mat. 4. Get thee hence, Satan. Prosit [ilegible] sternutatio [ilegible], Maldonate.

[ilegible] art an offence unto me] Thou doest thy good will to [ilegible] me in the course of my calling, as Mediatour, wherein, say some, he sinned more grievously then afterwards he did in denying his Master, and was therefore so sharply rebuked. So when ([ilegible]. Act [ilegible] Mon. fol. 1153.) [ilegible] was sollicited by Criton to break prison, and save his life by flight; Friend Criton, said he, thine earnestnesse herein were much worth, if it were consistent with uprightnesse: but being not so, the greater it is, the more trouble [ilegible]. I know not (said that [ilegible] Martyr) by what reason they so called them my friends, which so greatly laboured to convert (pervert) me. Neither will I more esteem them then the Midianites, which [ilegible] times past called the children of Israel to do sacrifice to their Idols.

But the things that be of men] Erewhile it was of Satan, now of [ilegible]. How [ilegible] is it to descry a devil in our best friends sometimes, as [ilegible] the French Martyr did in his parents? Satan suborns such as may do much with us, and works in them effectually for our hurt, as a Smith doth in his forge, Ephes. 2. 2. They were [ilegible], and thereby tormented, saith the Apostle of those [ilegible], Heb. 11. 37. Satan speaks to us sometimes by our friends, as thorow ([ilegible].) trunks and canes.

entries.title: Matthew 16:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not step before me, [ilegible] to me, as Peter attempted to do, whose fault herein is purposely recorded, that be might not be (as by the Papists, for [ilegible] ([ilegible].) respects, he is) over-much magnified, [ilegible], as is above observed, and made collaterall, a very copesmate to Christ himself.

Let him deny himself] Abdicet seipsum, Let him abrenounce himself flatly, peremptorily, again and again (as the word importeth) with a stout and stiff deniall to so unreasonable a request, as self will be sure to make to a man, his whole [ilegible] throughout. Every one hath many a self within himself to say nay to, though never so dear to him. Levi said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him, neither did he acknowledge his [ilegible], nor knew [ilegible] own children, that he might observe Gods Word, and keep his [ilegible], Deut. 33 9. This was much. But he that will be Christs Disciple, must do more then this. He must deny himself, his own reason, will, affections, appetite, aims, ends, acts, [ilegible], &c. He must utterly renounce himself, as much as if he had nothing at all to do with himself. Yea, he must condemn and cast away himself, as God doth those reprobates, whom he denieth, disowneth and disavoweth for ever. Horreo quicquid de meo est ut sim meus, saith Bernard. Ita cave tibi ut caveas [ilegible], saith another. So take heed to your [ilegible], that you take heed of your self. Oh misery! saith a third; we could not suffer a Lord, (O [ilegible] non [ilegible], conservo [ilegible]. mus. [ilegible]. [ilegible]. lib 12.) and yet we sustain to serve our fellow-servant, self. [ilegible] the Emperour dying, affirmed, that he was proud of one of his victories only, viz. That he had overcome his own flesh, that worst of enemies. Of all slaveries none so grievous to a good heart, as to be slave to himself. And this yoke of slavery, it is an easie matter to shake off, saith Seneca; but he is fouly deceived. For a man will sooner say nay to all the world, then to himself. This made Robert Smith the Martyr write thus to his wife, Be alwaies (Act. and Mon. [ilegible]. 1545.) an enemy to the devil and the world, but specially to your own flesh. There are some diseases that will not be cured, till we be let bloud ad deliquium animae, till the patient [ilegible]; and such is sin: it is corruptio totius substantiae, the sinner must be unmade, taken all asunder, ere the new creature can be made up in him: he must be stark dead to sin [ilegible] he can live to [ilegible], as S. Peter ([ilegible], 1 [ilegible]. 2. 24.) hath it: and the word he [ilegible] there implieth, that the old frame must be utterly [ilegible], and the whole man done to death, and [ilegible] for a whole burnt-offering. Instead of a [ilegible], saith Origen, we must kill our [ilegible] passions: in stead of a Goat, our unclean affections: in stead of slying fowls, our idle thoughts and evil imaginations. Loe this is that evangelicall sacrifice, that rationall service so much commended and called for, Rom. 12. 1. Do this, and thou shale live: leave it [ilegible], and thou art undone for ever. Pray therefore with him, Domine, libera me à malo homine, meipso, Lord, free [ilegible] from an ill man, my self.

And take up his crosse] Where [ilegible] is renounced, the crosse is [ilegible] born. It is self (saith one) [ilegible] the crosse pinch. Things puft up with winde, break when they come to the fire: so [ilegible] that are puffed up, and filled with self, will [ilegible] nothing. Privation is one of the principles of naturall generation, so is self-deniall of holy [ilegible]. Pain would this flesh make strange of that which the Spirit doth embrace (said M. [ilegible], Martyr, in a letter written to his wife out of the prison.) O Lord, how loth is this loitering [ilegible] to [ilegible] forth in Gods [ilegible]! It fancieth, (Act and [ilegible]. [ilegible].) forsooth, much fear of fray-bugs, &c. Take up the crosse, and follow me thorow thick and thin, thorow fire and water; Oh this is an hard saying, saith another Martyr. But if there (Ibid 1494.) be any way on horse-back to heaven, surely this is the way. Only we must take up our crosse, be active in it, and not stay till it be laid upon us, whether we will or no. And then bear it patiently, not grin under the burden of it, as antick pictures [ilegible] to do under the weight of the house-side, [ilegible] they are fastened. Drink [ilegible] Gods cup willingly, and at the first (saith M. Bradford) (Ibid. 1483.) and when it is full: lest peradventure if we linger, we drink at length of the dregs with the wicked, if at the beginning we drink not with his children. We must take up our crosses (saith another) and when God bids us yoke, he is the [ilegible] man that (M. [ilegible].) yeelds his neck most willingly.

And follow me] Without sciscitation; let him go blinde-fold ([ilegible] `[ilegible] [ilegible].) whether I lead him, as Abraham did. Neither may he leap over the hedge of the command, for avoiding the foul way of affliction, Sed [ilegible] quocunque Christus vocârit, [ilegible] in ea loca migrandum [ilegible] —Pigris ubi nulla campis ([ilegible] lib. 1 Od. [ilegible].) Arbor [ilegible] â recreatur aurâ; Quod [ilegible] mundi nebulae, malusque Jupiter urget.
